findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Scrutiny Management Board
findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: EHCP numbers in Sandwell forecast to grow from approximately 5,000 in 2025/26 to 9,500 or more by 2031/32
findings.detail: The paper says the EHCP cohort has grown by around 30% over the last year. It forecasts that around 33% of additional children will be eligible for home to school transport, creating a General Fund pressure of £7.7m in 2027/28.
findings.matters: EHCP growth drives both the High Needs deficit and the General Fund transport pressure, so it is the common root of the two largest SEND-related exposures in the paper.
findings.figures: approximately 5,000 EHCPs in 2025/26 to 9,500 or more by 2031/32; around 30% growth in the last year; 33% of additional children forecast eligible for transport; £7.7m SEND transport pressure in 2027/28
findings.quote: The number of children with EHCPs could grow from approximately 5,000 in 2025/26 to 9,500 or more by 2031/32.

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Scrutiny Management Board
findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: HRA reserves are forecast to fall below the required level around year 20 of the 30-year Business Plan, with the HRA moving into deficit by year 24
findings.detail: The paper says rent convergence and lower borrowing costs keep the HRA stable in the short term, but reliance on borrowing to fund investment in existing homes causes debt and interest costs to rise over time. A regional benchmark of £67,000 per property has been added for capital expenditure, a rise of £25,000.
findings.matters: A ringfenced housing account that does not balance over its 30-year plan, and depends on borrowing, is a risk other councils with large HRA stock are also modelling.
findings.figures: £67,000 per property capital benchmark, up £25,000; reserves below required level around year 20; HRA in deficit by year 24; £8.9m 2026/27 HRA reserve draw
findings.quote: This demonstrates that the HRA is currently not sustainable over the 30- year timeframe without further cost reduction measures

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Scrutiny Management Board
findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Employer pension contribution rate falls to 17.4% for the current three-year period from 24.6%, with 19.1% projected for the final two years of the MTFP
findings.detail: The paper says the rate is set by the triennial West Midlands Pension Fund valuation and that the outcome of the next valuation, due after 2028/29, is uncertain. The increase to 19.1% is a projection for the final two years of the MTFP.
findings.matters: The change in employer contribution rates moves the pay bill by a material amount, and councils in the same fund will face the same valuation outcome.
findings.figures: 17.4% contribution rate for the current three-year period; 24.6% for the period up to 2025/26; 19.1% projected for final two years of the MTFP; 3.6% per annum pay increase assumed
findings.quote: Therefore, contribution rates for the final two years of the MTFP are projected to increase to 19.1%.

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Scrutiny Management Board
findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: One-off £1.3m draw from earmarked reserves funded by Birmingham Airport dividends in 2026/27 is used to balance the 2027/28 budget
findings.detail: The paper says the council does not budget for airport dividends because timing and value are uncertain, so the windfall is treated as a one-year addition. It says the approach repeats the 2026/27 draft budget.
findings.matters: Using one-off dividend receipts to balance a recurring budget is a choice finance directors and lenders look at when judging whether a balance is structural.
findings.figures: £1.3m one-off draw in 2027/28; nil in 2028/29 to 2031/32
findings.quote: This would result in a draw from reserves of £1.3m in 2027/28 in order to help to balance the budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Draft revenue borrowing cost budget for 2027/28 is reduced to £23.8m, a £2.1m cut that leaves £3.9m of headroom for further project requests
findings.detail: The paper says the reduction is used to help balance the 2027/28 budget. It says borrowing costs remain within the council's 6% cap on net budget, and that surpluses or deficits on borrowing costs will move in or out of a Capital Financing earmarked reserve.
findings.matters: A one-off cut to the borrowing budget is a choice to draw on future capacity, and a lender or finance director will read the 6% cap and the headroom as the measures of how much further prudential borrowing the council can absorb.
findings.figures: £23.8m revised 2027/28 borrowing budget; £2.1m reduction; £3.9m headroom; 5.0% of net revenue budget in 2027/28; 5.4% in later years; 6% cap
findings.quote: it is possible to reduce the draft revenue budget for borrowing costs to £23.8m

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Scrutiny Management Board
findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Business rates system reset and revaluation took effect on 1 April 2026, with business rates income forecast at £167.4m in 2027/28 and £184.6m in 2031/32
findings.detail: The paper says the reset redistributes most of the growth accumulated under the previous system. It says the full effect on the council's business rates income is still uncertain and that the NNDR1 return due in January 2027 will confirm the 2027/28 figure.
findings.matters: Business rates reset and revaluation affect every council in the retention scheme at once, and a council retaining 100% of rates will see the change more directly than councils on 50% retention.

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Scrutiny Management Board
findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Council tax assumed to rise by 4.99% in 2027/28, generating £7.8m, with total council tax income growth of £8.4m including the tax base increase
findings.detail: The paper says the 4.99% assumption follows the prior year's February 2026 MTFP and is within the government's indicated cap. It says council tax income would total £165.0m, and that the figures for 2027/28 are provisional.
findings.matters: A council's willingness to use the full referendum limit is a funding decision that affects its gap and its political exposure, and it is a comparison other finance officers will make.

findings.headline: Social care budget growth of £20.0m is required in 2027/28, rising to £73.9m by 2031/32, the largest pressure in the MTFS
findings.detail: The paper says the adult social care forecast reflects demographic growth, more complex needs and external placement inflation. It forecasts the number of people requiring support could increase by around 16% by 2031.
findings.matters: Social care growth is the largest and fastest-growing line in the budget, and the same demand drivers are behind the pressures reported by councils across England.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit scheduled to transfer to General Fund from April 2028, with council facing approximately 10% of cumulative deficit as General Fund charge; amount unquantified.
findings.detail: The DSG reserve holds a deficit balance as at 1 April 2026, created by High Needs Block spending exceeding grant provision. Accounting regulations currently protect the General Fund (through March 2028), but the government has indicated it will fund 90% of High Needs Block deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28, leaving the council liable for approximately 10% of cumulative deficit. This will become a General Fund charge from April 2028 onwards, creating a future budget pressure of unspecified size that is not yet quantified in the council's financial planning.
findings.matters: High Needs Block deficits becoming General Fund liabilities represent a structural change in council finances; the timing creates a scheduled budget shock from April 2028 that concentrates financial stress in a defined period.
findings.figures: DSG deficit reserve balance at 1 April 2026: unspecified (recorded as 'deficit reserve balance'). Council liability: approximately 10% of cumulative High Needs Block deficit by end of March 2028; amount to be quantified.
findings.quote: As a result of the overspend relating to the High Needs Block in 2025/26, the council's DSG reserve has a deficit reserve balance as at 1st April 2026. There are currently accounting regulations in place until March 2028 that prevent the deficit becoming a charge on the General Fund. The government has stated that it is likely to fund 90% of local authority High Needs Block deficits to the end of 2025/26, and a similar arrangement is expected to be put into effect in relation to the 2026/27 and 2027/28 financial years, although this remains unconfirmed. Therefore there is likely to be a proportion in the region of 10% of the council's High Needs Block cumulative deficit at the end of March 2028 that will become a charge to the General Fund.

The updated 30-year business plan concludes the HRA is unsustainable without further unspecified mitigations.
findings.matters: HRA unsustainability with large and growing reserve draws represents a structural problem for the authority's housing function; this signals mounting pressure on housing maintenance and investment that cannot be sustained from rental income alone.

The February 2026 MTFS reported that the use of the reserve to balance the budget, at the levels forecast to be required in future years, is not sustainable in the medium-term. The HRA 30-year Business Plan has been updated to take account of revised forecast costs as well as income, and demonstrates that the HRA is not sustainable over the 30-year timeframe without further cost reduction measures and/or income generation measures being enacted.

Officers are required to complete the statutory NNDR1 return in January 2027, and the MTFP figures are described as 'the latest assumptions and are subject to change', with final update to come in February 2027.

findings.detail: The council is forecasting a cumulative DSG High Needs Block deficit of £40.753m at year-end 2026/27 (before accounting for the assumed High Needs Stability Grant of £5.448m, which would reduce this to £35.305m). A statutory override has protected councils from this deficit hitting the General Fund until March 2028. When the override expires, the council estimates around 10% of the cumulative deficit (approximately £3.5m+) will become a General Fund charge. The council notes it will be reliant on government providing additional High Needs Block funding both in the current year and future years, and that DSG allocations for 2027/28 are not yet known.
findings.matters: A forecast £35m+ structural deficit in school place-funding creates both a forward General Fund pressure from 2028/29 and an immediate cash flow impact (fewer resources available for council investment income), and is wholly contingent on government funding decisions outside the council's control.
findings.figures: £40.753m cumulative High Needs Block deficit forecast (pre-grant); £35.305m after assumed £5.448m High Needs Stability Grant; ~10% (~£3.5m) of cumulative deficit to become General Fund charge from March 2028; 2026/27 in-year overspend £34.700m
findings.quote: The council's cumulative High Needs Block (HNB) deficit is forecast to increase from £6.053m to £40.753m at year-end, taking account of the in-year forecast overspend of £34.700m... at the end of the statutory override, there is likely to be a proportion in the region of 10% of the council's HNB cumulative deficit at the end of March 2028 that will become a charge to the General Fund.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28-2031/32
findings.headline: HRA business plan shows long-term unsustainability with reserves forecast to fall below required level by year 20 and HRA moving to deficit by year 24
findings.detail: The council's updated 30-year HRA business plan, presented as part of the 2027/28 budget Star Chamber process, shows the HRA remaining stable short-term but becoming increasingly reliant on borrowing to fund investment in existing homes. Debt and interest costs rise significantly over time, causing reserves to fall below the required level around year 20 of the plan, and the HRA moves into deficit by year 24. The council states that rent convergence measures (allowing rents below formula rent to increase faster) will help increase income but alone will be insufficient to achieve long-term sustainability.
findings.matters: As one of England's largest council landlords, Sandwell's housing finance is a material asset management issue; an unsustainable 30-year business plan signals forward pressure on capital investment, borrowing capacity, and tenant affordability.
findings.figures: 27,700 council-owned homes; 30-year business plan shows reserves falling below required level around year 20 and HRA deficit by year 24
findings.quote: the revised model demonstrates that the HRA Business Plan remains stable in the short term, supported by rent convergence and lower borrowing costs. However, the Business Plan becomes increasingly reliant on borrowing to fund investment in existing homes, causing debt and interest costs to rise significantly over time. As a result, reserves fall below the required level at around year 20 of the plan, and the HRA moves into deficit by year 24. This demonstrates that the HRA is currently not sustainable over the 30-year timeframe without further cost reduction measures and/or income generation measures being enacted.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28-2031/32
findings.headline: Forward budget deficits reach £67.1m by 2031/32 even after approved savings proposals, rising from £16.2m in 2027/28
findings.detail: The council forecasts net deficits before savings proposals of £16.2m (2027/28), £29.3m (2028/29), £41.5m (2029/30), £53.6m (2030/31), and £67.1m (2031/32). Even after applying savings and income generation proposals of £16.2m, £23.1m, £26.5m, £21.7m and £23.1m respectively across the five years, revised deficits remain at £0m (2027/28 balanced), £6.2m, £15.0m, £31.9m and £44.0m. The 2027/28 balance is achieved through one-off measures including £12.1m reserve drawdown and £2.1m reduction to borrowing costs budget.
findings.matters: A council facing deficits that grow this steeply through the strategy period, inadequately addressed by available savings proposals, faces a fundamental planning gap and will need either further service reductions or income growth not yet identified.
findings.quote: Forecast Net Expenditure Requirement Prior to Mitigations 504.2 [2027/28] ... 621.4 [2031/32]; Revised Forecast Deficit - 6.2 15.0 31.9 44.0 [2028/29-2031/32]

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2027/28-2031/32
findings.headline: Adult social care and SEND demand pressures forecast to reach £73.9m cumulative growth by 2031/32, rising from £20m in 2027/28
findings.detail: Adult social care costs are increasing due to demographic growth (16% increase in people requiring support by 2031), more complex care needs, and inflation in external placement costs. External adult social care placements are forecast to increase 36% by 2031. SEND education, health and care plan cohorts have grown 30% in the past year and are forecast to grow from approximately 5,000 to 9,500 by 2031/32, with SEND transport costs rising from £7.7m in 2027/28. Together these account for over £27.7m of the £39.8m total investment required in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Demand-led service pressures this steep and extending this far forward present a fundamental challenge to medium-term financial sustainability and constrain discretionary spending for other services.
findings.figures: £20.0m adult social care growth 2027/28 rising to £73.9m by 2031/32; 16% forecast increase in people requiring support by 2031; external placement costs rising 36% by 2031; SEND EHCP cohort growing from ~5,000 (2025/26) to 9,500+ by 2031/32; SEND transport £7.7m in 2027/28 rising to £25.9m by 2031/32
findings.quote: Social care is the dominant and fastest-growing budget pressure, with budget growth of £20.0m required in 2027/28, increasing to £73.9m by 2031/32.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Treasury & Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Investment portfolio returned 4.10%, marginally above the 4.01% benchmark, on average balances of £79.7m
findings.detail: The council's investment strategy prioritised security and liquidity over yield. The portfolio was maintained short-term to cover cash flow requirements, with consideration given to placements up to 12 months with high credit-rated institutions. The 4.10% return slightly outperformed the benchmark of 4.01%, indicating competent treasury management of investment balances.
findings.matters: Returns on investment balances offset some of the cost of internal borrowing (borrowing from cash reserves rather than external markets). The benchmark outperformance is modest but shows the council is not losing return through conservative positioning.
findings.figures: Portfolio return 4.10%; benchmark 4.01%. Average balances invested £79.7m. Year-end investment balance £44.9m.
findings.quote: Returns on the investment portfolio have been marginally above benchmark with 2025-26 posting an average return of 4.10% (with average balances invested of £79.7m) against a benchmark of 4.01%.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Treasury & Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £35.7m in prudential borrowing caused the CFR variance, with works reprofiled into future years
findings.detail: The council forecast prudential borrowing of £69.066m in its February 2026 Treasury Management Strategy but only £33.383m was required. The difference is attributed to phasing delays and schemes not commencing as planned, with works being reprofiled into future financial years. Despite the slippage, the overall capital programme remained within approved budgets.
findings.matters: Capital programme slippage can indicate either disciplined project management or delays in delivering services to residents. A lender needs to understand whether delays are temporary repricing or signal broader issues with project delivery. The reprofiling defers the borrowing need but does not eliminate it.
findings.figures: Prudential borrowing actual £33.383m vs forecast £69.066m. Variance £35.683m (51.6% lower than forecast).
findings.quote: Key variances from the approved indicators in 2025-26 are due to the slippage of capital expenditure into future financial years due to phasing of works on schemes being reprofiled or schemes not commencing.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Treasury & Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Council took no material new external borrowing in 2025-26 due to inflated borrowing rates; instead took short-dated debt (2 months to 2 years) at rates 4.04–5.00% with view to future refinancing
findings.detail: Rather than lock in long-term debt at high rates, the council took short-dated borrowing from PWLB and other local authorities maturing between June 2026 and March 2028. This included £60m from PWLB (HRA and General Fund) and £50m from other local authorities (General Fund), all at rates between 4.04% and 5.00%. The strategy assumes rates will fall, allowing refinancing at better terms when debt matures.
findings.matters: This exposes the council to refinancing risk when the short-dated debt matures. If rates remain elevated or rise further, refinancing costs will be higher, pushing up future financing costs. It also shows the council is deferring the cost decision rather than locking in rates now.
findings.figures: New borrowing in 2025-26: PWLB HRA £40m at 4.04-4.10%; PWLB GF £20m at 4.30-4.33%; Other Local Auth GF £50m at 4.10-5.00%. Rates ranging 4.04% to 5.00%. Maturities 2 months to 2 years.
findings.quote: It was considered prudent to take short-dated debt with the view that at maturity it could be refinanced at a more preferential rate.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Treasury & Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: IFRS 16 Leases implementation added £14.567m to long-term liabilities, larger than the £6.995m initially forecast
findings.detail: The new accounting standard (effective 1 April 2024) required the council to recognise lease assets and future payment liabilities on the balance sheet. The actual movement was significantly larger than the initial forecast because the council lacked data to quantify the impact when the forecast was made. Liabilities are paid through annual unitary charges, lease payments, and service costs but have no impact on budgets.
findings.matters: This increases the reported liabilities on the council's balance sheet but does not represent new cash obligations—it is a reclassification of existing lease commitments. However, it materially affects balance sheet ratios and the CFR that lenders and auditors monitor, and the underestimation shows data weaknesses in the council's accounting systems.
findings.figures: Actual movement in other long-term liabilities (£14.567m); forecast movement (£6.995m). Difference of £7.572m larger than expected.
findings.quote: The movement in other long-term liabilities is larger than original estimates as these originally did not include values for the implementation of IFRS 16 – Leases due to us not having the data to quantify the financial impact.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Treasury & Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Council maintained under-borrowed position by borrowing internally from cash reserves rather than accessing external debt markets
findings.detail: The council's gross borrowing (£526.057m) remains below the Capital Financing Requirement (£904.045m), a strategic under-borrowed position of £377.988m. The council chose not to take new external borrowing despite capital financing needs, instead drawing on internal cash resources. This generates cash efficiencies in a high interest rate environment but requires careful cash management and monitoring of liquidity.
findings.matters: Under-borrowing can be prudent cash management in high rate environments but also represents deferred external borrowing costs. A lender needs to assess whether the council can sustain this position and whether refinancing risk is building as short-dated debt approaches maturity.
findings.figures: Over/(Under) Borrowing position: (£377.988m). Gross borrowing £526.057m vs CFR £904.045m. External borrowings £441.688m; other liabilities £84.369m.
findings.quote: For all financial years detailed above, the Council has held an under-borrowed position when comparing actual debt holdings to the Capital Financing Requirement. This is a strategic application of treasury cash management as the Council has borrowed "internally" from its cash investment resources, thereby reducing investment income opportunity but also not incurring increased debt costs.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Treasury & Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement closed at £904.045m, £43.3m below the February 2026 forecast of £947.300m
findings.detail: The council's underlying borrowing need for capital expenditure came in materially lower than forecast. Prudential borrowing was £33.383m against a forecast of £69.066m, primarily due to capital programme slippage and reprofiling. This was partly offset by larger-than-expected movements in other long-term liabilities (IFRS 16 Leases), which reduced CFR more than anticipated.
findings.matters: The CFR is the fundamental measure of a council's capital financing need. A lower outturn suggests better control and fewer borrowing requirements, reducing long-term debt servicing costs and refinancing risk.
findings.figures: Actual closing CFR £904.045m; February 2026 forecast £947.300m. General Fund: £322.979m (forecast £346.719m). HRA: £581.066m (forecast £600.581m). Prudential borrowing: £33.383m actual vs £69.066m forecast.
findings.quote: Amounts of prudential borrowing are lower than estimates for both General Fund and Housing Revenue Account due to slippage in the capital programme referred to earlier.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 - General Fund Capital Programme

findings.matters: The unexplained withdrawal of a £3.5m capital scheme raises questions about capital planning discipline, underlying project issues, or unplanned budget pressures. Lack of transparency on scheme changes affects confidence in the council's capital governance and financial planning.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 - General Fund Capital Programme

Persistent underdelivery over multiple years indicates operational capacity constraints or process issues within the council's housing function, which is a risk indicator for the council's ability to meet statutory obligations and manage service demand.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 - General Fund Capital Programme
findings.headline: Capital programme projected to underspend by £13.2m, representing 13% of revised budget.
findings.detail: The Grand Total shows a revised budget at Quarter 1 of £98.9m but forecast expenditure of only £85.7m, resulting in a variance of (£13.2m). With only 10% of spend completed in Quarter 1, the projected underspend is material and spread across multiple directorates, with only Children and Education forecasting on-budget delivery.
findings.matters: A 13% projected underspend indicates significant execution risk on the capital programme. Delayed capital delivery affects planned service improvements and infrastructure, and suggests potential capacity or governance issues in project delivery that would concern lenders assessing the council's financial management.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 - Collection Fund Monitoring

The council states much of this variance is covered by appeals provisions already set aside, and notes the underlying rateable value reduction of £0.4m is not material enough to warrant Medium-Term Financial Plan adjustments, though it will be monitored.

findings.quote: The data presented indicates that net business rates income is £5.2m lower than original estimates.  Much of this relates to adjustments in Rateable Value, as determined by the Valuation Office following appeals lodged by businesses.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 - Collection Fund Monitoring
findings.headline: April 2025 LCTRS change introduces new council tax liabilities for previously exempt households, creating collection risk
findings.detail: Changes to the Local Council Tax Reduction Scheme from April 2025 mean households previously not liable for council tax are now required to contribute. The paper explicitly flags this as presenting 'a risk to council tax collection rates, which continues to be monitored.' Collection behavior of these newly liable populations is unknown and could compound the existing declining collection trend.
findings.matters: Policy changes introducing newly liable populations with unproven payment behavior create forecasting uncertainty and downside risk to income, particularly when overall collection rates are already declining
findings.figures: Affects portion of approximately £189m total council tax liability issued

This presents a risk to council tax collection rates, which continues to be monitored.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 - Collection Fund Monitoring
findings.headline: Council tax collection declined to 26.9% in Q1 with forecast year-end of 89.3%, down from 91.7% the previous year
findings.detail: Quarter 1 2026/27 collection reached 26.9% of annual liability, below 27.6% in Q1 2025/26 and 27.9% in Q1 2024/25. The projected March 2027 collection rate is 89.3% versus 91.7% in 2025/26 and 93.2% in 2024/25, representing a material downward trend. The council attributes this to a worsening trend reflected nationally.
findings.matters: Declining collection rates reduce cash inflows, potentially forcing greater reliance on reserves or borrowing to manage cash flow, and signal growing collection difficulties among residents
findings.quote: Collection performance for 2026/27 is marginally below previous years and is following a worsening trend that is reflected nationally.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £8.4m General Fund and £28.8m HRA, with projects reprofiled into 2027-28.
findings.detail: General Fund capital expenditure was £63.8m against an approved forecast of £72.2m. HRA was £28.8m lower than indicator. The council attributes this to 'capital slippage into future financial years and not from project underspends,' with spending being 'reprofiled into 2027-28.'
findings.matters: Slippage defers borrowing costs but raises delivery questions. Given rising debt levels and increasing reliance on internal reserves, repeated slippage could indicate execution risk or optimistic planning assumptions.
findings.figures: General Fund £63.8m actual vs £72.2m forecast. HRA £28.8m below forecast.
findings.quote: General Fund outturn of £63.8m was lower than the original indicator of £72.2m. This is due to capital slippage into future financial years and not from project underspends.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26

The council justifies this as providing 'sufficient headroom for potential borrowing associated with the approved capital programme and treasury cashflow management.' Actual year-end debt was £488.2m.
findings.matters: An £80m increase in borrowing capacity, combined with planned reliance on internal reserves, signals the council expects to raise higher external debt in future years to fund capital investment.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council is using £378m of internal reserves to avoid external borrowing for £904m of capital needs.
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement (underlying borrowing need) totals £904.0m, but external debt is only £486.4m. The £378m gap is funded from internal cash and reserves. The report states the council is 'using a significant amount of internal borrowing to fund part of its CFR rather than external loans.'
findings.matters: Internal borrowing postpones external debt but depletes reserves. A lender needs to understand reserve adequacy and whether this strategy is sustainable if capital costs rise or future reserves cannot cover continued drawdowns.
findings.figures: CFR £904.0m, external debt £486.4m, internal borrowing £378.0m.
findings.quote: The gross debt is £378.0m lower than the CFR indicating that the Council is using a significant amount of internal borrowing to fund part of its CFR rather than external loans.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: External debt increased by £44.7m to £486.4m (8.7% year-on-year growth).
findings.detail: Treasury debt rose from £441.7m in the prior year to £486.4m at 31 March 2026. The council attributes this to borrowing for its capital programme, though actual capital expenditure was lower than forecast: General Fund spent £63.8m against an indicator of £72.2m.
findings.matters: A lender must track whether debt growth is sustainable. An 8.7% annual increase, coupled with capital programme underspend, suggests either catch-up borrowing is coming or execution is uncertain.
findings.figures: £486.4m (2026) vs £441.7m (2025). General Fund capex £63.8m vs £72.2m forecast.
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, Treasury Debt totalled £486.4m, compared with £441.7m in the prior year, showing an increase of £44.7m.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - General Fund Reserve Balances
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves are declining by approximately £25m in a single year
findings.detail: Total earmarked reserves (excluding school balances and general fund) fall from £207m to £182m, a reduction of nearly £25m. findings.matters: Rapid reserve depletion signals the council is using reserves to bridge the gap between spending and income. If this trajectory continues, reserves will exhaust within a few years, leaving no buffer for unforeseen pressures or downturns.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - General Fund Reserve Balances

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - General Fund Reserve Balances
findings.headline: Council has a specific reserve for savings plans it cannot deliver
findings.detail: Budget Monitoring - Savings Not Delivered holds £1.557m. This reserve is explicitly set aside to cover the fact that some of the council's planned savings are not materialising. The reserve is being held at the same level into 2026/27, suggesting ongoing slippage.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Q1 Budget Monitoring Report 2026/27
findings.headline: Savings delivery split 63% achieved, 17% with plans in place, 11% one-off only
findings.detail: The council rates savings delivery as 63% green (delivered), 17% amber (plans in place but not yet evidenced), and 11% blue (one-off in year). Managers have given assurance on amber savings, but the paper acknowledges 'there remains a risk that these savings could impact on the outturn position for 2026/27' if they are not delivered. The £0.623m overspend assumes the amber savings land.
findings.matters: Amber savings are assumed in the forecast but not yet proven. If even half the amber (8.5%) fails, the overspend doubles. One-off savings (blue) do not help in future years, leaving a structural gap.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Q1 Budget Monitoring Report 2026/27
findings.headline: General Fund balance at 5.0% of net budget (£22.799m forecast year-end), at the minimum of the council's 5–10% reserves policy range
findings.detail: After the £0.623m Q1 overspend, the General Fund balance is forecast to fall to £22.799m, which the council states equals 5.0% of the £464.480m net budget. This is at the lower end of the council's own policy range of 5–10% and matches independent guidance. The paper does not explicitly state whether the council considers this adequate given the identified SEND and adult social care risks.
findings.matters: A lender needs to see headroom in reserves to absorb shocks. Being at policy minimum with multiple emerging pressures leaves little margin if forecasts deteriorate further or if one-off issues arise.
findings.figures: General Fund balance £22.799m (forecast year-end); net budget £464.480m; represents 5.0% of budget; policy range 5–10%
findings.quote: Subject to audit of the council's accounts, at 1 st April 2026, the General Fund balance is £22.569m... which equates to 5.0% of the council's net budget in 2026/27. Independent advice is that General Fund unearmarked reserves should equate to 5% - 10% of net expenditure.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Q1 Budget Monitoring Report 2026/27
findings.headline: Capital programme experiencing significant slippage: £13.236m GF capital delayed into 2027/28, HRA programme £12.798m underspent due to contractor issues and project delays
findings.detail: The council revised the GF capital budget to £98.919m but forecast expenditure of only £85.683m, leaving £13.236m to be reprofiled into 2027/28. The HRA programme shows £12.798m underspend, with the largest variance (£7.244m) from the Tipton Regeneration Scheme, where 'issues relating to the main contractor have resulted in a forecast underspend'. Additional HRA slippage of £6.643m reflects schemes 'awaiting formal approval'.
findings.matters: Capital slippage can indicate delivery risk, and contractor issues on a major regeneration scheme are a red flag. The council is also facing Aids and Adaptations demand pressures (£1.7m overspend) which may indicate care/housing needs outpacing supply.

findings.quote: Capital expenditure is taking place more slowly than originally forecast, and budgets for several projects are expected to have to be reprofiled forward into 2027/28.

findings.committee: Cabinet
findings.paper_title: Q1 Budget Monitoring Report 2026/27
findings.headline: Sandwell Children's Trust carrying £18.2m cumulative deficit with Q1 overspend of £1.2m; council funding additional £6.597m in 2026/27 to offset part of deficit
findings.detail: The separate legal entity (wholly owned by the council) reported a deficit of £18.2m at end of 2025/26 due to 'higher than budgeted for children's social care placement costs', a problem flagged as national. In Q1 2026/27, SCT has already overspent by £1.2m on staff and placement costs. news_drafts.headline: Sandwell forecasts £34.7m schools grant overspend for 2026/27, all of it in high needs
news_drafts.lead:
Sandwell Council forecasts a £34.7m overspend for 2026/27 on its dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools. All of it is in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). The draft medium-term financial strategy puts the cumulative high needs deficit at £40.753m at year-end, up from £6.053m, and says demand for SEND services has risen beyond budgeted levels.

A statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps the deficit off the main balance sheet, runs to March 2028. The papers estimate around 10% of the cumulative deficit at that date is likely to become a charge to the General Fund, the council's main account for day-to-day spending. The cabinet report also gives a forecast budget pressure of £7.7m in 2027/28 on SEND home to school transport, because of rising numbers of children with education, health and care plans. It proposes £7.7m of ongoing growth for it.
